introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0580 Physics 1, June 2020, Ordinary Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Section 1 (questions 1 to 43) gives independent questions; Section 2 (questions 44 to 50) gives groups of questions on practical situations. Each question has four suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer. Non-programmable and cordless calculators are allowed.

**Useful constants:** acceleration of free fall $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; speed of light in vacuum $c = 3\times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; charge on an electron $e = 1.6\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$.
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D.

questions.enonce_markdown: The base unit of length is:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the International System of Units (SI) the base unit of length is the metre, symbol $\mathrm{m}$. The millimetre, centimetre and kilometre are multiples or sub-multiples of the metre, not base units. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a physical quantity?
questions.corrige_markdown: A physical quantity is something that can be measured and is expressed as a number together with a unit. "Metre" and "joule" are only units (no number), and "100" is only a number (no unit). "3 seconds" has both a numerical value and a unit: it is a value of the physical quantity time. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A body is taken from the equator to the North Pole.
questions.corrige_markdown: Mass is the amount of matter in the body, so it does not change when the body is moved. Weight is $W = mg$, and the gravitational field strength $g$ is slightly larger at the poles than at the equator (the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles and its rotation reduces the effective $g$ at the equator). So the mass stays constant while the weight increases a little. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Its mass decreases and its weight remains constant
Its mass remains constant but its weight increases
Its mass increases and its weight remains constant
Its mass and its weight both remain constant

questions.enonce_markdown: A ball is thrown downward at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from a roof $10\ \mathrm{m}$ high. Its velocity when it reaches the ground is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$ with $u = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $h = 10\ \mathrm{m}$:

$v^2 = 5^2 + 2\times 10\times 10 = 25 + 200 = 225$, so $v = \sqrt{225} = 15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The trap is option B ($\sqrt{2gh} \approx 14$): it forgets the initial velocity of the ball. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An experiment is carried out to determine the acceleration of free fall by timing the direct fall of a steel ball, from an initial velocity of zero through a given height. The equation of motion that is used to process the data collected in the experiment is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The quantities measured are the height $s$ and the time of fall $t$, and the ball starts from rest ($u = 0$). The equation that links $s$, $t$, $u$ and $a$ is $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, which becomes $s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $g = \frac{2s}{t^2}$. The other equations all contain the final velocity $v$, which is not measured in this experiment. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Energy is defined as:
questions.corrige_markdown: Energy is the ability (capacity) to do work. Option A is the definition of power, option B is the expression for efficiency, and option C is the inverse of the efficiency of a machine (work output divided by work input would be the efficiency). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A stone of mass $0.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ is moving with a velocity of $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. How much kinetic energy does the stone possess?
questions.corrige_markdown: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times 0.2\ \mathrm{kg}\times (20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2 = 0.1\times 400 = 40\ \mathrm{J}$. The trap is to forget to square the velocity (that gives $2\ \mathrm{J}$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following energy sources are all renewable sources?
questions.corrige_markdown: A renewable source is replaced naturally within a human lifetime. Wood and animal waste (biomass) can be regrown or produced again, and wave energy is renewable. In B, uranium is a finite nuclear fuel; in C, coal is a fossil fuel; in D, petrol is a fossil fuel. Only option A contains renewable sources only. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A machine has a velocity ratio of $9$ and needs an effort of $10\ \mathrm{N}$ to lift a load of $50\ \mathrm{N}$. The efficiency of the machine is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Mechanical advantage $= \frac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \frac{50}{10} = 5$.

Efficiency $= \frac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}}\times 100\ \% = \frac{5}{9}\times 100\ \% = 55.6\ \%$.

Option A ($\frac{1}{9}$) and option B ($\frac{1}{5}$) come from using only one of the two ratios. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When a trumpet and a guitar are used to play the same musical note a difference is noticed. This difference is due to the:
questions.corrige_markdown: Two instruments playing the same note have the same fundamental frequency, so the same pitch. What differs is the quality (timbre) of the note, which depends on the number and relative strength of the overtones (harmonics) each instrument produces along with the fundamental. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A ray of light from a raybox is directed into a rectangular glass block as shown in Figure 1.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

Angles of incidence $i$ and corresponding angles of refraction $r$ are measured. The graph of $\sin i$ (y-axis) against $\sin r$ (x-axis) obtained from this experiment is (Figure 2, options A to D):

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: By Snell's law, $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n$, a constant (the refractive index of glass), so $\sin i = n\sin r$. The graph of $\sin i$ against $\sin r$ is therefore a straight line through the origin with a positive gradient equal to $n$. In Figure 2 this is graph C. Graph A is a curve, graph B is a horizontal line (constant $\sin i$) and graph D has a negative gradient. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An object is placed at a point beyond $2F$ from a converging lens. The image formed is:
questions.corrige_markdown: For a converging lens, an object beyond $2F$ gives an image between $F$ and $2F$ on the other side of the lens. This image is real (it can be formed on a screen), diminished (smaller than the object) and inverted. A same-size image occurs only when the object is at $2F$, and a virtual, magnified, erect image occurs when the object is between the lens and $F$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The primary coil of a transformer is often wound on the secondary coil so as to prevent:
questions.corrige_markdown: Winding the primary coil over the secondary coil makes sure that nearly all the magnetic flux produced by the primary passes through the secondary, so that little flux is lost (flux leakage, that is, loss of flux linkage). Resistance losses are reduced by using thick copper wire, and hysteresis and eddy current losses are reduced by the choice and lamination of the iron core. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The numerical value of absolute zero in degree Celsius is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Absolute zero is $0\ \mathrm{K}$, which corresponds to $-273\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (since $T/\mathrm{K} = \theta/^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When a radioactive atom undergoes beta decay:
questions.corrige_markdown: In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron (the beta particle), which is emitted. The number of protons goes up by 1, and because a neutron has been replaced by a proton the total number of nucleons stays the same. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the proton number decreases by 1 and the nucleon number remains the same
the proton number increases by 1 and the nucleon number remains the same
the proton number remains the same and the nucleon number decreases by 1
the proton number remains the same and the nucleon number increases by 1

questions.enonce_markdown: A cellulose acetate rod rubbed with cloth:
questions.corrige_markdown: Only electrons can be transferred by rubbing (protons are fixed in the nuclei). Cellulose acetate loses electrons to the cloth, so the rod is left with a deficit of electrons and becomes positively charged. Options A and C involve the movement of protons, which does not happen, and B has the wrong sign. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: gains protons and becomes positively charged
gains electrons and becomes negatively charged
loses protons and becomes negatively charged
loses electrons and becomes positively charged

questions.enonce_markdown: Electromotive force (EMF) is measured in:
questions.corrige_markdown: EMF is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge, so it is measured in joules per coulomb, which is the volt. Newtons measure force, amperes measure current and joules measure energy. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The effective resistance of a $12\ \Omega$ resistor and a $6\ \Omega$ resistor connected in parallel is:
questions.corrige_markdown: For resistors in parallel $\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1+2}{12} = \frac{3}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$, so $R = 4\ \Omega$. The trap is option A, which forgets to invert $\frac{1}{R}$; option D is the series value. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A $2400\ \mathrm{W}$ electric iron is used at maximum output for $6$ hours in a month. If the cost of a unit of electricity is $60$ FCFA, how much will the user pay as electricity bill for that month?
questions.corrige_markdown:
One unit of electricity is $1\ \mathrm{kWh}$. Power $= 2400\ \mathrm{W} = 2.4\ \mathrm{kW}$.

Energy used $= 2.4\ \mathrm{kW}\times 6\ \mathrm{h} = 14.4\ \mathrm{kWh}$.

Cost $= 14.4\times 60 = 864$ FCFA.

Option A is the result of a factor $10$ slip, and option D ($6\times 60$) forgets the power of the iron. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the distance between two charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ is doubled, the electrostatic force of repulsion between them will:
questions.corrige_markdown: By Coulomb's law, $F = \frac{kQ_1Q_2}{d^2}$, so the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance. If $d$ is doubled, $F$ becomes $\frac{1}{2^2} = \frac{1}{4}$ of its original value: the force reduces. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An open can containing a little water is heated until the water boils. The can is then closed tightly and cold water poured on the can. The sides of the can collapse because:
questions.corrige_markdown: After boiling, the can is full of steam. When the can is sealed and cooled, the steam condenses into a small volume of water, so the pressure inside drops rapidly. The atmospheric pressure outside, which is unchanged, is now larger than the pressure inside and crushes the sides of the can. The external pressure does not increase, so B is wrong. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following instruments is an application of Hooke's Law?
questions.corrige_markdown: Hooke's law states that the extension of a spring is proportional to the force (load) applied, within the elastic limit. A newton meter (spring balance) uses exactly this: the extension of its spring is proportional to the force and is read on a scale. A manometer uses a liquid column, a beam balance compares weights, and a Bourdon gauge measures pressure by the uncurling of a curved tube. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When a bucket full of water is being pulled out of a well, it appears lighter when it is still in the water than when it is out of water. The "apparent lightness" is caused by:
questions.corrige_markdown: When the bucket is in the water, the surrounding water exerts an upward force on it, the upthrust (buoyancy), equal to the weight of water displaced. This upthrust partly balances the weight, so a smaller force (tension) is needed to hold it and it feels lighter. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following physical quantities has newton-metre as the unit?
questions.corrige_markdown: Work $= \text{force}\times\text{distance}$, so its unit is $\mathrm{N\,m}$ (a joule). Momentum is in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ (or $\mathrm{N\,s}$), pressure in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (pascal) and power in $\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ (watt). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 3 shows a tin of milk rolling down an inclined plane. In the figure four forces are shown on the tin: $P$ (along the slope, pointing up the slope), $Q$ (vertically downward), $R$ (along the slope, pointing down the slope) and $S$ (perpendicular to the slope, pointing away from it).

![fig-3](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

The force which prevents the tin from sliding is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The force that opposes the sliding of the tin down the slope is friction between the tin and the plane. Friction acts along the surface in the direction opposite to the motion or tendency to slide, that is, up the slope. This is the arrow $P$. $Q$ is the weight, $S$ is the normal reaction of the plane, and $R$ points down the slope (the component of the weight along the slope, which tends to make the tin slide). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A ripe mango falls from a tree $32\ \mathrm{m}$ tall. If its initial velocity is zero, the time it takes to reach the ground is:
questions.corrige_markdown: With $u = 0$, $s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $t = \sqrt{\frac{2s}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times 32}{10}} = \sqrt{6.4} = 2.5\ \mathrm{s}$ (using $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$). Options A and B are the values of $2s$ and $t^2$, obtained by stopping before the square root. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 4 shows how the displacement of an object in the direction of a force applied varies with the force.

![fig-4](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

The shaded area under the graph represents:
questions.corrige_markdown: The graph plots force (vertical axis, in $\mathrm{N}$) against displacement (horizontal axis, in $\mathrm{m}$). The area under a force-displacement graph is $\text{force}\times\text{distance}$, which is the work done by the force (in joules). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The best reason why aluminium is often preferred to steel in the construction of aircraft is that aluminium:
questions.corrige_markdown: An aircraft must be as light as possible. Aluminium (and its alloys) has a much lower density than steel, so a part of the same size is much lighter while still strong enough. Resistance to rusting is an advantage but not the main reason, appearance is irrelevant and a higher mass per unit length would make the aircraft heavier. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: has a higher mass per unit length

questions.enonce_markdown: An electromagnetic radiation which is emitted from the nucleus of an atom is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves emitted by an unstable nucleus when it rearranges, usually after alpha or beta decay. Alpha radiation is a stream of helium nuclei (particles, not electromagnetic waves). X-rays come from electron transitions or from electrons hitting a target, and infrared radiation comes from the vibrations of atoms and molecules. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: It is not possible to predict which atom of a particular radioactive sample will decay. This is because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Each unstable nucleus has the same chance of decaying in a given time interval, and there is no way to know when a particular nucleus will decay: the decay is random. This is why we can only predict the behaviour of a large number of atoms (through the half-life). "Spontaneous" means that decay is not affected by external conditions, which is a different property. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: radioactive decay is a random process
radioactive decay is a spontaneous process
during radioactive decay the mass of the radioactive isotope reduces
the half-life of a particular radioisotope is constant

questions.enonce_markdown: The specific heat capacity of a material depends on the:
questions.corrige_markdown: The specific heat capacity $c = \frac{Q}{m\,\Delta\theta}$ is the energy needed to raise the temperature of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the material by $1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. It is a property of the substance itself (water, copper, iron...), so it depends only on the nature of the material, not on how much energy is supplied, on the mass or on the temperature change. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: thermal energy gained by the material

questions.enonce_markdown: When one end of an iron rod is held in the hand and the other end is inserted into a flame and left there for a few minutes, heat energy soon reaches the hand by:
questions.corrige_markdown: In a solid metal rod, heat travels from the hot end to the cold end by conduction: vibrating atoms and free electrons pass energy along the rod. Convection happens only in fluids (liquids and gases), and radiation does not need a material medium and is not how heat travels along the rod. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: On a certain filament bulb is written $220\ \mathrm{V}$, $80\ \mathrm{W}$. The resistance offered by the filament when a current of $4/11\ \mathrm{A}$ flows through the main supply is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The current is $I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{80}{220} = \frac{4}{11}\ \mathrm{A}$, which agrees with the value given. The resistance of the filament is

$R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{220}{4/11} = 220\times\frac{11}{4} = 605\ \Omega$.

(Check: $R = \frac{V^2}{P} = \frac{220^2}{80} = 605\ \Omega$.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following elements should be added to germanium to produce a p-type semiconductor?
questions.corrige_markdown: A p-type semiconductor is made by doping a Group IV semiconductor such as germanium with a Group III element, which has only three outer electrons and creates "holes". Boron is a Group III element. Phosphorus (Group V) would give an n-type semiconductor, copper is a metal and silicon is itself a semiconductor of Group IV. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following quantities determines the loudness of a sound?
questions.corrige_markdown: The loudness of a sound depends on the amplitude of the sound wave: the larger the amplitude, the more energy the wave carries and the louder the sound. Frequency determines the pitch and overtones determine the quality (timbre). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The critical angle for a ray of light incident in water at a water-air boundary is $47.8^\circ$. The refractive index of water is:
questions.corrige_markdown: For a ray going from water to air, $n = \frac{1}{\sin C} = \frac{1}{\sin 47.8^\circ} = \frac{1}{0.7408} = 1.35 \approx 1.4$. Option A ($0.7$) is $\sin C$ itself, without taking the inverse. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When the net force acting on an object reduces, the acceleration of the object:
questions.corrige_markdown: By Newton's second law, $a = \frac{F}{m}$: for a constant mass the acceleration is directly proportional to the net force. If the net force reduces, the acceleration reduces. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the graphs in Figure 5 represents a velocity-time graph for an object accelerating uniformly from rest?

![fig-5](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Uniform acceleration from rest means $v = at$, which is a straight line through the origin with a positive gradient. This is graph D. Graph A shows a uniform deceleration, graph B a constant velocity, and graph C a straight line that does not start at the origin (the object already has an initial velocity). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Heavy duty vehicles usually have large and broad tyres. Of what advantage is this?
questions.corrige_markdown: The force on the road is the weight of the vehicle and does not change. Pressure is $p = \frac{F}{A}$, so broad tyres, which have a large contact area, give a small pressure on the road, which reduces damage to the road surface and prevents the vehicle from sinking. A is wrong because the force stays the same, and a wider base increases the stability. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: To exert a small force on the ground
To support the heavy weight of the vehicle
To exert a small pressure on the road
To reduce the stability of the car

questions.enonce_markdown: The electromotive force of a cell is given as $1.5\ \mathrm{V}$. This means that the cell can supply:
questions.corrige_markdown: $1\ \mathrm{V} = 1\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$: an EMF of $1.5\ \mathrm{V}$ means that the cell supplies $1.5\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy to each coulomb of charge that passes through it. The EMF does not fix the current (A) or the total energy (B), and "energy per ampere" (C) is not a correct unit combination. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: $1.5\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy per ampere of current
$1.5\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy per coulomb of charge

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following devices is a rectifier?
questions.corrige_markdown: A rectifier changes alternating current into direct current. A diode conducts in one direction only, so it blocks half of each a.c. cycle and is used as a rectifier. A rheostat and a resistor control current and a transformer changes the value of an a.c. voltage. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the radiations or particles below is most ionising?
questions.corrige_markdown: Alpha particles are heavy and carry a charge of $+2$, so they knock electrons off many atoms in a very short distance: they are the most ionising (and the least penetrating) of the three. Beta particles are less ionising, and X-rays and gamma rays are weakly ionising. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the graphs in Figure 6 is the velocity-time graph for a body falling freely in air, and attaining a terminal velocity?

![fig-6](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: At the start the body accelerates at about $g$ (steep gradient). As it speeds up, air resistance grows, the net force and the acceleration decrease, so the gradient of the graph decreases until the air resistance equals the weight. Then the acceleration is zero and the velocity stays constant (terminal velocity): the graph curves and levels off. This is graph B. Graph A is a constant acceleration (no air resistance), C is a decreasing velocity, and D shows an increasing acceleration. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 shows the setup used to determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid.

![fig-7](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to:

*Options as printed:* A) raise a unit mass of the liquid by one degree Celsius; B) change a unit mass of the liquid to gas at constant temperature; C) raise the temperature of the liquid by one degree Celsius; D) raise the temperature of a unit mass of the liquid by one degree.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The specific heat capacity of a substance is the energy needed to raise the temperature of a unit mass (1 kg) of the substance by one degree ($1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ or $1\ \mathrm{K}$): $c = \frac{Q}{m\,\Delta\theta}$, in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,^\circ C^{-1}}$.

Option B describes the specific latent heat of vaporisation, and option C leaves out the unit mass. Options A and D both express the correct definition: A names the unit "Celsius" but omits the word "temperature" ("raise ... by one degree"), and D names the temperature and the unit mass but omits "Celsius". The printed key cannot be fixed with certainty between A and D, so this question is left without a designated letter.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 shows the setup used to determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid.

![fig-7](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

The two other important items necessary for the experiment but that are NOT shown in the setup are:
questions.corrige_markdown: The heater has a known power rating $P$, so the electrical energy supplied is $E = Pt$, which needs the time $t$: a **stopwatch**. The energy gained by the liquid is $E = mc\,\Delta\theta$, so the mass $m$ of the liquid must be known: a **scale balance**. The thermometer for $\Delta\theta$ is already in the figure. A voltmeter and an ammeter are not needed because the power of the heater is known. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 shows the setup used to determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid.

![fig-7](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

Lagging is used in the experiment in order to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Lagging is a poor conductor (insulator), which reduces the heat lost to (or gained from) the surroundings so that nearly all the energy from the heater goes into the liquid. It cannot prevent the exchange completely, so "reduce" (B) is correct and "prevent" (A) is too strong. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: prevent heat exchange with the environment
reduce heat exchange with the environment
increase heat exchange with the environment
prevent direct contact between the inner container and the outer container

Figure 7 shows the setup used to determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid.

![fig-7](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

A similar setup can be used to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block. The item in the setup above that will NOT be needed is the:
questions.corrige_markdown: The stirrer is used to spread the heat evenly through the liquid. A solid metal block cannot be stirred, and its heat spreads by conduction, so the stirrer is not needed. The lagging is still needed to reduce heat losses and the thermometer is still needed to measure the temperature rise. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 shows a rectangular coil WXYZ carrying a current and located between the pole pieces of a horse-shoe magnet.

![fig-8](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

When current flows through the coil in the direction shown in the diagram, the coil:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The pole piece on the left is S and the one on the right is N, so the magnetic field between them points from N to S, that is, to the left. The current flows from W to X (side WX, away from the viewer) and from Y to Z (side YZ, towards the viewer).

By Fleming's left-hand rule (first finger = field to the left, second finger = current, thumb = force): on side WX the force is **upward**, and on side YZ, where the current is reversed, the force is **downward**.

The two opposite forces form a couple: the left side goes up and the right side goes down, so the coil turns clockwise as seen from the front. The coil does not move bodily into or out of the page because the forces on the two sides are equal and opposite. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 shows a rectangular coil WXYZ carrying a current and located between the pole pieces of a horse-shoe magnet.

![fig-8](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

The direction of the force acting on the rectangular coil, WXYZ, was determined using:
questions.corrige_markdown: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (motor effect) is found with Fleming's left-hand rule. Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of an induced current (generator), the right-hand grip rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a current, and Faraday's law gives the size of an induced EMF. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 shows a rectangular coil WXYZ carrying a current and located between the pole pieces of a horse-shoe magnet.

![fig-8](gce-ol-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

The motion of the coil WXYZ can be decreased by:

*Options as printed:* A) using a larger coil; B) having fewer turns of coil; C) using a weaker magnet; D) reversing the magnetic pole pieces.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The force on each side of the coil is $F = nBIl$, where $n$ is the number of turns, $B$ the magnetic flux density, $I$ the current and $l$ the length of the side in the field. The turning effect (and so the motion) decreases if $n$, $B$, $I$ or $l$ is reduced.

A larger coil increases $l$, so it increases the motion. Reversing the pole pieces only reverses the direction of the turning. Having **fewer turns** (B) and using a **weaker magnet** (C) both decrease the force, so both are correct and the question has no single correct key. No letter is designated.
